articles.title: Líderes discursam na sessão de alto nível da COP31; acompanhe ao vivo
articles.summary: Lula foi anunciado no momento previsto para seu discurso, mas não falou. Mais cedo, discursou na abertura da Cúpula dos Líderes e, rouco, pediu ao ministro do Meio Ambiente que lesse outra fala.
articles.body:
Lula foi anunciado no momento previsto para seu discurso, mas não falou. Mais cedo, discursou na abertura da Cúpula dos Líderes e, rouco, pediu ao ministro do Meio Ambiente que lesse outra fala.

A sessão de alto nível da COP31, com pronunciamentos de chefes de Estado e de governo, foi encerrada nesta quarta-feira (11). Lula chegou a ser anunciado, mas não discursou. Mais cedo, o presidente brasileiro havia falado na abertura da Cúpula de Líderes.

O presidente de Palau, Surangel Whipps Jr., discursa agora na sessão de alto nível da COP31.

Lula, que estava previsto para falar antes dele, chegou a ser anunciado, mas não discursou. Ainda não há confirmação de quando o presidente brasileiro poderá fazer seu pronunciamento.

Pela ordem provisória da ONU, o pronunciamento nacional de Lula deveria ocorrer neste momento na sessão de alto nível da COP31. O presidente chegou a ser anunciado, mas não discursou.

Mais cedo, Lula falou na abertura da Cúpula de Líderes e, devido à rouquidão, pediu que o ministro do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, João Paulo Capobianco, lesse outro discurso durante um encontro sobre florestas.

Agora discursa Alexander Van der Bellen, presidente da Áustria. Pela lista provisória da ONU, Lula é o próximo a falar na plenária da COP31, caso a sequência seja mantida.

O presidente das Maldivas, Mohamed Muizzu, discursa neste momento na COP31. Segundo a lista provisória da ONU, o próximo a falar é o presidente da Áustria, Alexander Van der Bellen, seguido pelo presidente brasileiro, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. A ordem dos pronunciamentos pode sofrer alterações.

Agora discursa Denis Sassou Nguesso, presidente da República do Congo.

Agora discursa Alexander Stubb, presidente da Finlândia.

O presidente do Sudão, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, discursa neste momento na sessão de alto nível da COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. Lula também está na lista de líderes que devem fazer pronunciamentos nacionais nesta quarta-feira (11).

'Cada fração de grau importa', alerta presidente da Comissão Europeia

Ursula von der Leyen chamou o último verão europeu de “ verão da verdade ”, ao lembrar do calor extremo e da alta dos preços da energia.

Ela alertou que o mundo caminha para ultrapassar o limite de aquecimento de 1,5°C.

A dirigente também afirmou que a União Europeia deve reduzir suas emissões em mais da metade até 2030. Mas projeções oficiais apontam um corte de 54%, abaixo da meta de 55%.

A presidente da Comissão Europeia, Ursula von der Leyen, discursa neste momento na plenária da COP31, em Antália, na Turquia.

A presidente da Tanzânia, Samia Suluhu Hassan, discursa neste momento na plenária principal da COP31, em Antália. É a quinta chefe de Estado a falar nesta quarta.

Embora cada país tenha três minutos, os discursos têm se estendido, e a fila avança mais devagar que o previsto. O presidente Lula é o 20º da lista e, no ritmo atual, deve discursar no fim da tarde no horário local, início da tarde em Brasília.

Em outro momento do discurso, Lula afirmou que a COP31 terá a missão de “devolver à mudança do clima a atenção que ela merece”. Leia como foi o discurso completo.

Lula afirmou que a crise climática também é uma crise de justiça de classe, gênero e raça, além de refletir desigualdades entre os países. Segundo o presidente, não faz sentido abandonar o princípio das responsabilidades comuns, porém diferenciadas, já que os países ricos se desenvolveram às custas do planeta e precisam cumprir seus compromissos.

O presidente também destacou que a próxima COP, em solo africano, representa uma oportunidade histórica para garantir mais recursos a um continente que, segundo ele, se encontra estrangulado.

"O Brasil vai fazer sua parte. Adotando o mapa do caminho para reduzir a dependência de combustíveis fortes e eliminar o desmatamento e a degradação da floresta", diz.

O presidente afirma ainda que o planeta não pode ficar à mercê de disputa de hegemônicas. "Secas, enchentes, incêndios e elevação do nível do mar já fazem parte da realidade das pessoas".

"No início deste ano, a mudança do clima desapareceu dos discursos e dos documentos das lideranças globais", afirma o presidente. Lula disse ainda que "passamos a falar mais de armas do que sobrevivência da futura gerações".

Bom dia, o presidente do Brasil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, começa o seu discurso na COP31.

articles.title: Joe Biden, in His Only New Interview, Goes on Camera with PEOPLE to Talk About Everything (Exclusive)
articles.summary: Speaking with PEOPLE at his home in Wilmington, Del., the former president opens up about living with stage 4 prostate cancer, revelations in his new memoir...
articles.body:
Joe Biden gets candid about his stage 4 prostate cancer as he releases his new memoir , Promise Me, America

The former president reflects on life, withdrawing from the 2024 race and the legacy he hopes to leave

Dr. Jill Biden describes the daily realities of caring for her husband with support from their family

Two days after the Democrats swept the midterm elections , former President Joe Biden has that signature twinkle in his blue eyes.

"Look at the people we got elected: first women governors, first Black governors," he tells PEOPLE with a quiet rasp.

At 83, and living with stage 4 prostate cancer — for which he completed radiation and is undergoing hormone therapy — Biden is slower than when he suddenly withdrew from the presidential race in 2024 following a disastrous debate against Donald Trump and amid concerns about his health. Still, his perennial optimism remains.

"I'm not saying I'll live forever," says the one-term president, seated in the dining room of his Wilmington, Del., lake house, "but the point is that I have all my faculties, I have access to all the things I had before and I feel good."

He's fighting the disease "like hell," Biden writes in his presidential memoir, Promise Me, America , out Nov. 17. Through it all, his wife, Dr. Jill Biden , 75, has been by his side. Being a family caregiver — like 63 million Americans — is "emotionally, physically hard," the former first lady says after returning home from volunteering at a women's prison, where she teaches literature part-time.

Although she has help looking after her husband and says family is a constant at the house, "My days are making sure he eats right. Does he exercise? Is he taking the right medicine? Did I talk to the doctor?"

Reality came into focus when she read a magazine at a nail salon and imagined traveling to the destinations on the glossy pages. "All of a sudden it struck me, like, 'Wait a minute, this isn't our life now,' " she says. "We're on a new journey."

With no questions off the table, President Biden addresses his life and health now, his presidency and the legacy he hopes to leave behind.

In May 2025, 118 days after you left office, you announced that you had been diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer that had spread to your bones. You write that you're fighting it with the "help of an incredible medical team and an even better family." What does that fight look like?

It looks very positive. There's a lot of people who've been diagnosed with cancer, particularly the kind of cancer I have, who live long lives, who live for another 10, 20 years. And so far, the two tests that have been done show that the cancer is not metastasized beyond what it already was ... There are eight different pills I take a day.

Next June will mark your 50th wedding anniversary. What has cancer taught you about your marriage that you didn't know before?

Nothing. I knew from the beginning what she was. Jill is, first of all, bright as hell. Secondly, I think she's the most beautiful woman in the world, which every husband probably thinks, but I believe it. And we have a real partnership.

How has your family, including your grandchildren and your great-grandchild, supported you?

They're always here. "Can we come up, Pop? Pop, can we do this?" I do more with my grandchildren than I do with anybody else, and that's for real. I'm interested and they're interested in serious things as well ... They're involved in a lot of things having to do with public service. They participate in a number of issues that relate to the well-being of the country. They're the loves of my life.

As the second Catholic to become president, you've been candid about how your faith has guided you through hard times. Do you still see signs of those you've lost?

I do. I see signs of their love in their progeny. I see signs of their love of things that I find out that they have done that I didn't know they had done before ... My son Hunter , he and his brother Beau were born a year and a day apart. They're each other's best friends in the world. When Beau died, it was a blow to Hunter in a way that was almost beyond repair ... Now he's deeply involved in public policy things. He's deeply involved in making the case, but he's straight as an arrow in terms of his alcoholism. My dad used to have an expression: "Joey, family's the beginning, the middle and the end." And that's how it is.

You write, "People say I was deluding myself that I could do the job [of president] at my age. My answer to that is: I was doing the job." Why do you think they felt that way?

It's natural. If tomorrow you're going to say that the head of your [company] is going to be hired on as an 80-year-old person, you go, "What the hell's going on?" But the value I think I brought was I knew so many of the leaders, I knew their inclinations, I knew what was going on, and many of them came to me. I thought it was value added, not subtracted.

Standard medical guidelines don't recommend routine prostate cancer screenings for men over 70. You write, "I was treated no differently from any other 82-year-old man in America. Maybe I should have been." What do you say to Americans who believe that a screening should have been part of your annual physical?

Look, White House doctors are doing what the whole entire medical profession is doing ... I had some discomfort, and Jill thought, Why isn't that test done for men who are in their 70s? And there wasn't any particular [sign] except recurring pain.

You describe a "cynical twist" on your cancer news: that some folks said you hid your cancer as president. Why do you think they reacted that way?

A lot of people do that. They hide bad news from the public if they're elected officials. I didn't do that. We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on. I think it's important for a national leader, as president, to let people know they go through some of the very same things that a lot of American people are going through ... I wasn't hiding it at all.

Many have spoken about the toll of the Presidency. How might your undiagnosed cancer have exacerbated that?

First of all, I never felt the toll. I read [others] like Harry Truman talk about [how] it's the most difficult job in the world. I didn't find it that way. And so I, quite frankly, found that it didn't in any way interfere with my job.

What do you miss the most about the job?

The staff, the people in the White House. They're good people, from the people making sure there's a sheet on the bed to the people who are taking care of all the visitors that come through. They all have a sense of honor, what they're doing in the White House. It's the People's House.

What's your reaction to the Trump ballroom and the East Wing being destroyed?

Almost as disturbing as the gold bars on the walls of the White House and the Oval Office. I mean, what the hell are we talking about? I find it disturbing ... I've viewed the president's judgment in tearing down the East Wing and a number of other things as nothing more than to try to create monuments to himself: "I built that." I find it beneath the country.

It's been two years and four months since that debate moment on the stage with Trump. What is your perspective on it now?

Look, I don't know anybody who hasn't made a mistake in a debate. To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there'd be another debate, which there wasn't. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn't another debate, it didn't disturb me because it wasn't consequential.

In hindsight, looking at the 2024 election, is there anything you would've done differently?

What I can't say, because there's no evidence of it — if I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have resigned. I would've not gone forward, because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for [president]. But that wasn't the case ... I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job.

Hunter has been speaking out on podcasts and social media. What do you make of that?

Hunter is one of the brightest men I know. He has more moral and physical courage than most people I know, and I'm really proud of him. He's making the case as to how we should proceed as a country.

He's said of the pardon you gave him: "Was it good for our Constitution? Was it good for the American people? Was it good for my father's legacy? No on all accounts." What's your perspective?

I disagree ... I watched the modus operandi of Trump. He goes after people without any basis, whether they're viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do. If I hadn't pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who's dealt with me—he would go back and try to do harm to them, as I've observed.

In your book, for the first time, you share the letter that Trump left you in the Oval Office after you beat him in the 2020 election. Your takeaway: "It was almost as if there were two Donald Trumps." What do you mean?

That could have been written by President Kennedy to me or by President Johnson or by George Bush. I mean, it was gracious, it was generous, and it was totally inconsistent with the kind of president he'd been.

You write, "Promise me, America, that we will be the nation we know in our hearts we can be and should be." What does that nation mean to you at 83, after more than 50 years of public service?

It means to continue to hold those truths to be self-evident, that we're all created equal. I got involved in politics because of the Civil Rights movement. It means to be engaged in trying to help make the country a better place than it has been, to give people the benefit of the doubt ... When I say, "Promise me, America," I mean, America, you know the promises we made. Let's keep them.

How do you want the American people to remember you?

I tell you, it's the greatest honor any man or woman could be given anywhere to be the President of the United States of America. And I hope I kept the promise of America ... I didn't say I didn't make mistakes—but I meant what I said, and I did what I said I was going to do.

articles.title: White House confronts Democrats over planned probes, claiming possible 'criminality'
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that su...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress -- may amount to "blatant criminality."

White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

Garcia most likely would chair the powerful panel in the new Democratic-controlled Congress that is seated in January. Garcia warned Trump officials to "lawyer up" as his party was on the way to stunning victories in last week's midterm election.

In response, Scharf wrote that "threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality." The letter's existence was first reported by Punchbowl News.

Garcia said in response to the letter that "it appears Donald Trump has something to hide" and stressed that Congress' investigative powers do not need the "permission of the White House."

"Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate," Garcia said. "The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse."

Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.

Garcia also wants to look at the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations . Other targets include Trump's White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family's role in mineral deals and Trump's crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that "there could be" a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying "Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it's through subpoenas or letters — so we're not going to stop working with Congress."

"Nothing I've said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise," he added.

Some lawmakers cautioned Democrats as well as the White House against overreaching.

Outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Trump critic, said he hopes Democrats don't squander their new powers on "stupid things."

"I hope they have real hearings about real things, not another Russiagate," he said, referring to a previous congressional inquiry into ties between Trump's first presidential campaign in 2016 and Russia. Trump repeatedly denounced that investigation as a "hoax."

"I think there is some real corruption there around the fringes," Massie said about Trump and some of those around the president. Massie lost his primary election to a Trump-backed GOP challenger.

Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., who is expected to be the next House Ethics Committee chairman, said he would not back down from any investigations because of warnings from the White House.

"If they're trying to intimidate, at least for me, it's not going to get me," said DeSaulnier, who was a Republican before he switched to the Democratic Party in 2000. "I don't work for a mafia, a mob organization."

Associated Press writer Eric Tucker and AP video journalist Nathan Ellgren contributed to this report.

articles.title: Surrealista: pierde un partido por golpearse la zapatilla con la pala
articles.standfirst: Nuria Rodríguez y Giulia Dal Pozzo cayeron ante Claudia Jensen y Tamara Icardo, pero el desenlace del encuentro quedó marcado por la decisión arbitral tras un gesto de la primera
articles.summary: Nuria Rodríguez y Giulia Dal Pozzo cayeron ante Claudia Jensen y Tamara Icardo, pero el desenlace del encuentro quedó marcado por la decisión arbitral tras un gesto de la primera
articles.body: La jornada de este miércoles en el Dubái P1 dejó una de las escenas más llamativas de la temporada en Premier Padel. Nuria Rodríguez y Giulia Dal Pozzo se despidieron del torneo en los dieciseisavos de final tras perder por 6-2 y 6-3 frente a Claudia Jensen y Tamara Icardo. Sin embargo, más allá del resultado, toda la atención se centró en una acción que terminó por decidir el encuentro de una manera inesperada. Con Jensen e Icardo a un punto de cerrar el partido, Rodríguez protagonizó un gesto de frustración al golpearse la zapatilla con la pala. La jugadora española ya había recibido una advertencia anteriormente y el árbitro interpretó que aquella acción merecía un segundo warning. Al acumular dos avisos, la sanción implicaba la pérdida automática del punto y, por tanto, el final del encuentro. La resolución sorprendió a las cuatro jugadoras, especialmente por el momento en el que se produjo. Rodríguez mostró inmediatamente su desacuerdo y comenzó a reclamar explicaciones al colegiado. Incluso Claudia Jensen, desde el lado contrario de la pista, pareció no entender la decisión y salió en defensa de la española con una frase contundente: "No es warning". La reacción de la gaditana reflejó la impotencia que sintió al ver cómo el partido terminaba de aquella forma. Con las manos en la cabeza y visiblemente afectada, la española no ocultó su frustración y volvió a hacer referencia a los problemas que, según ella, viene arrastrando con el arbitraje. "Siempre me pasa a mí, te juro que me quiero esconder. Siempre me pasa a mí", expresó Rodríguez, incapaz de encontrar una explicación a lo sucedido. La jugadora continuó mostrando su incredulidad por una sanción que consideraba desproporcionada. "Una pena. No sé cómo lo hago", comentó mientras trataba de asimilar que el desenlace del partido hubiera llegado por una decisión disciplinaria. También cuestionó directamente la interpretación del árbitro y el motivo por el que su gesto había sido considerado merecedor de una segunda advertencia. "Escúchame, ¿cómo puede ser? No puede ser por hacer así. ¿Estamos diciendo algo fuera de lo normal?", protestó durante la discusión. El principal argumento de Rodríguez giraba en torno a la necesidad de mantener una interpretación uniforme de las normas durante los encuentros. "Tienes que tener un criterio. Es que se equivoca todo el rato", insistió, dejando patente su malestar con la actuación arbitral. Lo ocurrido en Dubái no es un caso aislado en la temporada de Nuria Rodríguez. La jugadora ya había protagonizado otro enfrentamiento con el arbitraje durante el London P1 del pasado agosto, cuando competía junto a Giulia Dal Pozzo frente a Marta Ortega y Sofía Araújo. En aquel encuentro se produjo una situación controvertida con una pelota que inicialmente había sido señalada como mala. Tras recurrir a la revisión de vídeo, la acción terminó considerándose buena, aunque la árbitra decidió repetir el punto en lugar de concedérselo a Rodríguez y Dal Pozzo. La resolución provocó una larga discusión sobre la pista y fue necesaria la intervención del supervisor para intentar reconducir la situación. La tensión fue tal que la española llegó a plantearse abandonar la competición si se repetían episodios de ese tipo. Finalmente, fueron Marta Ortega y Sofía Araújo quienes optaron por conceder voluntariamente el punto a sus adversarias

articles.title: Ilhan Omar appears clueless on basis for federal probes: ‘You probably have more details on that’
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar told reporters she was never informed what federal agencies are specifically investigating, even questioning if multiple probes exist.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., told Fox News Digital on Tuesday she was never informed by federal agencies of the grounds on which she is being investigated — even claiming she isn’t sure how many probes into her there are. "No, no," she said when asked if she had been told exactly the basis for the investigations. There are two known ongoing federal probes into the Somali-born congresswoman — the first, confirmed by sources to Fox News Digital, is the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) looking into whether her immigration paperwork was fraudulently filled out by herself or her father; and the second is investigating her financial disclosures discrepancies and was confirmed publicly by U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro. ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS On Omar’s first day back on Capitol Hill following the investigations, she told Fox News Digital she doesn't know if DHS and the Department of Justice (DOJ) are each investigating her independently. "I’m not sure," Omar said. "You probably have more details on that." The congresswoman's feigned innocence on the matter came after she had a two-hour meeting with her lawyers at her Capitol Hill office on Tuesday. The news of the federal investigations first gained steam after Fox News Digital first reported that agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) were executing a federal raid on Omar’s Washington, D.C., residence on Oct. 12. Sources confirmed the search was in relation to an investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork. The Somali-born lawmaker arrived in the U.S. in 1995 as a refugee fleeing civil war after spending four years in a refugee camp in Kenya. ILHAN OMAR HUDDLES WITH HER DC-BASED LAWYERS DURING HER FIRST DAY BACK ON CAPITOL HILL AMID FEDERAL PROBES Federal agents reportedly seized the congresswoman’s cellphone, passport and computer. Fox News Digital also later confirmed that a sample of the congresswoman’s DNA was also obtained during the raid. Omar told Fox News Digital on Tuesday that "most" of the items seized during the raid have been returned to her possession. "I’ve gotten most of them back," Omar said. More information continues to come to light as the investigations proceed, including a federal court filing identifying Omar by the name "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi," which matches the last name of her ex-husband, whom reports have alleged is her brother. The marriage continues to draw scrutiny after the Daily Caller recently reported that her ex-husband Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, who is alleged to be her brother, described himself as a "gay man" in an academic paper that was published earlier this year. OBAMA ADMIN FIRST LAUNCHED THE INVESTIGATION INTO ILHAN OMAR'S ALLEGED BROTHER MARRIAGE Omar ignored Fox News Digital’s questioning about her ex-husband and rumored brother referring to himself as "gay" in Aug. 2026, just months before HSI raided her house and federal investigations got underway. The congresswoman is still under investigation as she returns to Capitol Hill after winning re-election to represent Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District. Her two high-profile lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, were seen leaving her office in the Longworth House Office Building after a roughly two-hour meeting.
